question: Comment: building fund
text:
Obviously the shul is ready to expand and this will cost a lot. However, the way the shul approached it seems unorganized and didn’t consider the financial situation of the community at large. Why is it that we haven’t seen one fundraising initiative outside of a large bill? 

There are many ways to fundraise and entice people to donate with events, dedications, and advertising. Asking for a SUGGESTED DONATION from members should be a last step after you already raised money, got people excited about the project, and know exactly how much you still need. People who can afford it will gladly pay extra to dedicate every door and bench. Those that are struggling won’t feel obligated to pay and will be more likely to donate if their situation improves. We may even donate our time or connections, if you don’t push us away. 

Donating to the shul is a choice that people make based on their financial capabilities. This is not a rich community. Many of the shul members can’t afford to own their own homes or struggle to pay a monthly mortgage. Even basic shul membership is a choice that is not easy to make. When we see a bill for the equivalent of 3 months rent on top of the membership we struggle to pay, it causes a lot of unnecessary anxiety, guilt and embarrassment. (Obviously we are obligated to pay this amount, but a unsettled bill still makes us feel like crap)
quote: People who can afford it will gladly pay extra to dedicate every door and bench.

question: Comment: current building
text:
The lack of adequate social hall space is one of the biggest shortcomings of our current building. We have a growing community with countless Bar Mitzvahs, Bat Mitzvahs, Kiddushim and other simchas, yet we lack the space to properly accommodate them. Even our regular weekly Kiddushim are constrained by the limited space, with a very small dedicated area for Kiddush preparation, setup, or serving, making an already crowded environment even more difficult to manage.

Beyond the obvious benefit to our members, this represents a significant missed revenue opportunity for the shul. A larger, more functional social hall, with proper space for Kiddush preparation and service, would allow us to host more events, encourage families to celebrate their milestones within our community and generate meaningful additional income for the shul.

Additionally, the 8:15 minyan is consistently packed on a weekly basis and has clearly outgrown its current space. We should be planning not just to accommodate its current attendance, but to allow room for continued growth. A larger, dedicated space would make a meaningful difference for those who attend regularly and ensure we aren’t limiting the minyan’s potential simply because of physical constraints.

question: Comment: current building
text:
1) The dumpster is worth every penny, that is a GOOD system for trash, let's keep that going. If we can do a similar thing for recycles, kol hakavod.

2) The ghosts in the mens bathroom are definitely keepers.  If you know, you know.  I actually miss them during the week when I'm at work.

3) I am 100% in favor of making our building safer and using grant money for updates that are needed. However, (ironically) I think the change in windows could have been made in a more transparent way.  I don't recall being asked how I would feel about glass you can't see out of and that don't really let light in. Shul feels a little like a fishbowl now and I try not to think about it, so if we do have a chance to rethink how the main sanctuary will look and feel, I say PLEASE let natural light in with normal windows. I am glad that we are safer and I respect that some of my friends needed that sense of security to feel comfortable in Shul.  That being said, I am a daily shul goer and I don't like the way it looks and feels now, so I would have appreciated the opportunity to weigh in on that decision before it was made and implemented.  Same with the doors.  There was nothing wrong with them before, except that they weren't bullet proof.  Then we got these fancy doors that have many problems and seem to not be bulletproof either.  I just think these changes that affect the regular experience of being in Shul should be made by more than a few people, and I do understand that it is intended for safety and there's no way to know before we do it - yes. And still, I am an average guy who goes to Shul every day and thought it was better with windows I could see out of and doors that didn't creak or break or need constant maintenance.  I just would have liked some input beforehand.  Thanks :)

4) We need another book shelf in the Beit Midrash area, but we also don't want to fill it up with stuff we don't need/want. So maybe just keep this in mind as an idea for now.

Okay, so now here are two concerns that may not be super relevant but they are building related.  (1) The Ner Tamid, if we can lose the large gold flappy pieces and just stick with the glass I think it would be much nicer, but that's just my opinion and likely not what you wanted to hear about. Also, (2) the structure of the Aron can accommodate Torahs wearing crowns, I think we should just leave the crowns on while they're in the Aron since it is actually big enough. Then there doesn't need to be a whole production of putting them on for two minutes and taking them off again, just have the Torahs always wearing them, which ultimately feels more kavodik to me.  Again, just my opinion.

question: Comment: anything else
text:
1) Many shuls have [something like] a wall with cubbies that members can be assigned and/or rent to keep some thing like tefillin or stuff for children or whatever in the shul. I didn't see that on the survey but I and many others would greatly benefit from that.
2) Our shul currently has all the main room lights on one switch. This means on tisha bav we cannot dim the lights. Though we hope not to need it, please install the lights on multiple switches (or with a dimmer?) for better tisha bav eve experience.
3) While the eruv is usually up in town, statistically sometime in the lifetime of this building it will be down on a shabbos when there's a simcha. Spend a little time now to avoid a headache later by thinking about how the shul property can easily be encased in an eruv so things can still function at shul. Much like thinking about how the sukkah will fit in, sometimes a small adjustment or extra gutter or whatever can make things much easier later.
4) For landscaping, consider installing two small fruit trees. Consult with a landscaper obviously what species are best, but it's a great opportunity to make birkas hailanos centrally accessible to all. We all know most people won't go find somewhere else to say it if not during kiddush with the text available right there.
